sections.overview: This nocturnal nightjar ranges from South and Southeast Asia to northern Australia; in Singapore it remains a resident in forests, scrub and parks.
sections.identification: Its mottled brown, grey and black plumage resembles leaf litter and bark, while white patches at the wing and tail tips become conspicuous in flight.
sections.habitat: It uses open forest, scrub and wooded parks, resting motionless by day on the ground or lengthwise along a branch where its camouflage is effective.
sections.diet: Like other nightjars, it catches insects in flight after dusk; museum stomach records also include worker ants taken on the ground, an unusual supplementary foraging mode.
sections.behavior: It is strictly nocturnal, and its cryptic daytime posture makes it easy to overlook even in settled parks.
sections.reproduction: In Singapore it lays one or two eggs directly on the ground in a shallow scrape, without building a nest; both sexes have been reported sharing incubation.
sections.ecology: It belongs to Caprimulgus, the nightjar genus that also includes the European Nightjar (C. europaeus); the two are relatives with broadly similar nocturnal insect-hunting habits but occupy different regions.
sections.conservation: The global assessment lists it as Least Concern; this broad category does not remove the value of local forest and scrub habitat.
